hints: Break the term apart - what does re-combine suggest about putting pieces of something together, and what molecule is being worked with here?
Think about where those pieces come from and what tools are used to cut, join and carry DNA into a new organism to make it transgenic.
walkthrough:
What recombinant means**
Think of DNA as an instruction manual. Recombinant means you take a page from one manual and insert it into a different manual, so the new manual contains a combination that did not exist before.

How it is done and why**
In this case the insect-resistance genes SN and Bt or OCII come from a different source to the potato. They are cut and joined using enzymes and carried into potato cells using vectors, so the potato becomes genetically modified and can make a new insect-poisonous protein.
Final answer: DNA from two different sources / species is joined / combined, using enzymes / vectors, to create a GMO / transgenic organism.

hints: Look at the difference between variety A and variety B - they share SN but differ in the second gene, so what question would a scientist want to answer by testing both?
walkthrough:
Why make two versions**
Variety A has Bt and variety B has OCII. You cannot know in advance which insect-killing protein will work best in potato leaves against Colorado beetle larvae, so you make both and compare them side by side under the same conditions.
Final answer: To test / compare the effectiveness of the different genes / proteins / Bt and OCII / varieties A and B to see which works better.

hints: Think about what would happen if all larvae died even without any new genes - how would you prove the deaths were really caused by the GM proteins?
walkthrough:
The need for a baseline**
The non-GM potatoes have no new insect-poisonous proteins. If larvae die on GM plants but 0% die on non-GM plants, you can be confident the deaths are due to the new genes and not to handling, time, or something else in the setup.
Final answer: To act as a control / provide a baseline for comparison.

hints: Start by describing the trend in Table 4.1 for A, B and non-GM at 24 h, 48 h and 72 h without jumping to a conclusion about food yet.
Link larval death to what happens to leaves and therefore to potato yield - why does killing a leaf-eater matter for food production?
Compare A versus B directly to decide which variety a farmer should choose to get the most food the fastest.
walkthrough:
What the data show**
Both GM types kill larvae while non-GM kills none. Variety A reaches 50% dead at 24 h, 93% at 48 h and 100% at 72 h. Variety B reaches only 37% at 24 h, 70% at 48 h and 93% at 72 h. Non-GM stays at 0% throughout.

Link to yield**
Colorado beetle larvae eat leaves, which reduces photosynthesis and so reduces tuber growth and crop yield. By killing the larvae, the GM plants protect their leaves, so more potatoes survive to harvest, increasing the food supply to help meet global demand.

Choose the best variety**
Variety A kills a higher percentage at every time and reaches 100% kill by 72 h, so it works faster and more completely than B. Growing variety A would therefore give the greatest protection and the most extra food.

Final answer: Both GM varieties A and B kill larvae, so less leaf damage occurs and yield of potatoes / food increases; variety A is best / kills most / fastest and should be grown to provide most food.
